newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Turkey says omens not good for ties with Greece.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says omens not good for ties with Greece.

text.p: Turkey said on Monday the omens were not good for any improvement in relations with its traditional rival Greece, accusing Athens of distorting facts and making unjustified allegations.

The two countries have a long history of enmity despite the fact that both are NATO members. Both Athens and Ankara have warned of the dangers of war in the Eastern Mediterranean or over the Aegean Sea, causing alarm in allied capitals.

Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller told the U.N. General Assembly her country wanted a peaceful resolution of all disputes. Ankara had hoped for more productive relations with the new Greek government after elections this month.

"Unfortunately, the recent statement of the Greek foreign minister from this very rostrum ... does not bode well," she said. "Distortion ... as well as unfounded allegations will not serve the creation of a climate of confidence..."
Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos attacked Ankara in a speech to the annual U.N. assembly last week, accusing it of breaking international law and of stoking tensions.
Ciller called for the U.N.-sponsored peace process on the divided island of Cyprus to move ahead quickly and criticised Greek Cypriots for provoking recent clashes there.
Turkey invaded the independent island in 1974 and seized the northern third, where some 30,000 Turkish troops are stationed, in response to a coup attempt by Greek Cypriots.
Moreover, Greek and Turkish forces almost clashed in January in a dispute over an uninhabited island.
With tensions running high between Athens and Ankara, Washington stated its concern and its intention to take a more active role in a note to Pangalos last week.

Tension in Turkey rose on Monday when Islamist urban guerrillas threw a grenade at the Ecumenical Orthodox Patriarchate, the seat of Patriarch Bartholomeos I who is spiritual leader of 250 million Orthodox Christians.

Ciller also repeated that Turkey would do everything necessary to prevent Kurdish rebel attacks launched from northern Iraq, saying it would not allow the area to be used as a base for such operations.

The Turkish government launched a big offensive against Kurdish rebels in southeastern Turkey last week and Ankara has said it reserves the right to set up a "security zone" in northern Iraq to protect its own borders, following the recent turmoil in the region.

"Turkey will not tolerate terrorist elements using Northern Iraq to stage terrorist acts against its territory," Ciller said. "We are determined to take all necessary measures to protect our legitimate security interests..."
More than 20,000 people have died in the 12-year-old conflict between Turkish security forces and the rebels fighting for Kurdish self-rule in the southeast.
